newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Weak start delivers disappointing Australia budget.
newsitem.headline: Weak start delivers disappointing Australia budget.

text.p: A weak starting point and a slow run-up for new fiscal cuts explain why the Australian government's underlying deficit for the coming fiscal year will be a disappointingly large A$3.9 billion.
Economists had expected a deficit for the year to June 1998 near A$2.5 billion.
But the starting point for that year was A$4.2 billion, not the A$3.7 billion that the market had figured and the government has not done much to reduce it.
The budget's underlying measures -- that is, excluding asset sales -- will save just A$352 million in 1997/98, not the A$1.0 to A$1.5 billion that had been hoped for.
The real thump in the budget is in the following year, when measures save A$1.9 billion, pushing government finance's into the promised underlying surplus, estimated at A$1.6 billion.

The main measure is the replacement of the planned government contribution to retirement savings (superannuation) with a cheaper tax break on savings, and it has a big impact: A$729 million in 1998/99, rising to A$1.9 billion two years later.
On the spending side there has been the usual multitude of minor cuts: A$15 million cut from child care here, A$50 million saved on rural assistance there.
The government is also finding an extra A$150 million year from foreign companies controlled by Australians and a one-off A$330 million from changed withholding tax arrangements.

Driven by such savings, the budget will power into underlying surpluses -- that is, excluding asset sales -- of A$5.4 billion in 1999/00 and a colossal A$10.6 billion in 2000/01, according to government estimates.
Fiscally, the budget is a much smaller affair than last year's, which implemented savings of A$3.9 billion in the first year rising to A$7.2 billion in the second.

Although the deficit for the current fiscal year is better than forecast in the January mid-year review -- A$6.9 billion rather than A$8.5 billion -- the boost has not flowed into an improved starting point for 1997/98.
Government officials said one of the main reasons for this discrepancy was that some 1996/97 spending had been deferred into 1997/98, boosting one year at the expense of the other.
Moreover, the projected 1997/98 dividend from the Reserve Bank of Australia had been marked down since the mid-year review.
The bank is now expected to pay A$1.2 billion in 1997/98, although officials would not say how much had been budgeted in the mid-year review, from a forecast A$2.1 billion in 1996/97.

The budget papers also show that the 1997/98 starting point has lost A$209 million in prospective revenue since the mid-year review because of so-called parameter variations, meaning the economy will not produce as much tax as expected.

Adding in asset sales and the like, the budget will be in so-called headline surplus in 1996/97 and throughout the forecasting period to 2000/01, showing that Canberra will have A$30 billion available to retire debt in the coming four years.
The 1996/97 surplus is projected at A$764 million, even though the A$3.3 billion proceeds from the privatisation of three airports will not be banked until 1997/98.
With the airport money and, more importantly, some of the proceeds from selling a third of Telstra Corp AOT.AX, the 1997/98 budget will shoot towa9 settle back to A$5.8
billion in the following year and rising to A$11.1 billion the year after that.
